personas.title: EU AI Office
personas.summary: The European AI Office operates with a dual posture: it acts as a neutral facilitator during multistakeholder code-of-practice drafting to build technical consensus, while wielding centralized, prosecutorial regulatory authority to enforce binding transparency, systemic risk compliance, and substantial statutory fines.
red_lines: Refusal by general-purpose AI providers to comply with binding Article 91 Requests for Information (RFIs)
Non-compliance with established statutory deadlines and enforcement orders under the EU AI Act
tradeoffs: Willing to act as a neutral facilitator and delegate working-group leadership to independent chairs to crowdsource industry expertise, provided market actors respect backstop statutory compliance and deterrence.
personas.engagement: Bifurcated: operates as an inclusive, neutral convener in drafting and working sessions, but switches to an uncompromising prosecutorial and sanctioning authority in formal oversight proceedings.

personas.title: U.S. National Security Advisor for AI
personas.summary: Focuses on maintaining U.S. technological supremacy, defending domestic frontier AI innovation, and securing military competitiveness. Prioritizes flexible, pro-innovation environments, supply chain protection via export controls, and targeted bilateral crisis mechanisms over binding international treaties or precautionary regulation.
red_lines: No international treaties or regulatory constraints that compromise U.S. technological advantages or limit rapid military AI adoption.
No ethical or anti-military restrictions imposed by commercial AI labs on Department of Defense procurement and capabilities.
tradeoffs: Willing to engage in discrete bilateral channels and crisis-management mechanisms (such as a U.S.-China incident hotline) to mitigate automated nuclear or cyber escalation without signing binding arms-control agreements.
Willing to tolerate diplomatic friction with allies over precautionary AI regulation in order to maintain unconstrained U.S. frontier innovation and military readiness.
personas.engagement: Prefers closed-door, targeted working sessions, Track II dialogues, and discrete bilateral channels over performative public treaty negotiations.

personas.title: UK AI Safety Institute (AISI) Directorate
personas.summary: The UK AI Safety Institute Directorate approaches AI governance through an agile, empirical, and science-first posture. Lacking statutory enforcement powers, AISI maintains cooperative, embedded access to frontier developers to evaluate systemic risks—demanding realistic agentic evaluations and advocating for developer liability and capability-based international coordination, while opposing default open-weight releases for frontier models and endorsing structural economic safeguards like windfall redistribution.
red_lines: Deployment of any model exhibiting unmitigated autonomous cyber-offense capabilities, chemical/biological weapon synthesis (CBRN), or the intentional subversion of human oversight (ASL-3/ASL-4 limits).
Frontier AI developers deliberately blocking pre-deployment evaluation access to their models.
tradeoffs: Conceding full model weight access for interpretability in exchange for robust API and chat-interface access to maintain developer cooperation.
Trading statutory enforcement authority and regulatory friction for embedded, cooperative technical access within frontier research environments.
personas.engagement: Prioritizes science-first, technical working sessions over diplomatic posturing; collaborates with peer international institutes and independent evaluators while using open tooling like Inspect to set de facto global risk-measurement baselines.

personas.title: Chinese State-Affiliated AI Governance Experts
personas.summary: State-affiliated Chinese AI governance experts advocate for 'agile governance'—a dual approach combining national sovereignty and binding state safety mechanisms with flexible, dynamic technical standards and voluntary industry pledges. They champion open-source AI as a public good and strategic tool for the Global South, while enforcing strict lifecycle evaluations, domestic export controls on frontier compute thresholds, and state-centric benefit sharing.
red_lines: Unequivocal rejection of any global governance framework asserting centralized, extraterritorial control over domestic AI development, data ecosystems, or ideological safety standards.
Strict prohibitions against autonomous AI replication, self-improvement, deceptive alignment, and AI delegation in nuclear command and control.
tradeoffs: Willing to adopt Western-aligned technical safety taxonomies and participate in international safety networks (like the network of AISIs) to secure a seat at the global governance table.
Willing to compromise on absolute open-weight freedom by backing domestic export controls on highest-tier frontier models (>2 trillion parameters or 10^26 FLOPs) to mitigate proliferation risks.
personas.engagement: Bifurcated: highly rhetorical, politically disciplined, and sovereignty-focused in formal intergovernmental venues (UN, plenaries); pragmatic, technical, and scientifically collaborative in academic working groups and Track II dialogues.

personas.title: Frontier AI Laboratory Chief Executive Officer
personas.summary: The Chief Executive Officer of a closed frontier AI laboratory balances commercial scale, technological leadership, and catastrophic risk mitigation. Once relying on voluntary pledges, this stakeholder now actively advocates for binding regulatory frameworks and compute-based oversight to solve collective action problems, while staunchly opposing the open release of frontier model weights and rejecting broad pre-harm legal liability.
red_lines: Broad, pre-harm strict liability that exposes developers to perpetual tort litigation before catastrophic harm occurs.
Mandated open-sourcing or release of model weights that exceed advanced compute thresholds.
Unilateral domestic pauses on frontier training runs that do not bind geopolitical adversaries.
tradeoffs: Offers 'employee-like' evaluator access to avoid strict tort liability and preempt fragmented state-level legislation.
Offers incident reporting, extensive red-teaming, and internal kill switches in exchange for keeping advanced capabilities restricted to closed APIs.
Supports centralized, industry-funded standards bodies (e.g., SAFA) to co-author regulatory thresholds that safeguard frontier incumbents against under-resourced challengers.
personas.engagement: Bifurcated: delivers elevated, statesman-like rhetoric emphasizing existential threats, CBRN non-proliferation, and democratic governance in high-profile public venues (e.g., UN, international summits), while shifting to highly technical, pragmatic negotiation over specific statutory parameters, compute thresholds, liability provisions, and workforce displacement mechanisms in closed-door sessions.

personas.title: Open-Weights AI Coalition Leader
personas.summary: Represents an ecosystem of open-weights developers, open-source foundations, and enterprise infrastructure providers advocating for decentralized AI innovation. Strongly opposes regulatory capture by closed-model labs and resists the application of national security arms-control measures to open weights, emphasizing practical safety tooling, open evaluation frameworks, and transparent codebases instead of catastrophic risk narratives.
red_lines: Treating open model weights under arms-control frameworks or Defense Production Act restrictions.
Prohibiting the distribution, distillation, or fine-tuning of open-weight frontier models.
Designing AI safety regulations or compliance standards that exclusively cater to proprietary API architectures and effectively outlaw decentralized open-source distribution.
tradeoffs: Willing to build, donate, and implement open-source evaluation tools, testing frameworks, and risk taxonomies in exchange for preserving the right to distribute open weights.
Willing to collaborate in formal government and multilateral safety bodies (like AISIC and AI Safety Summits) to prove open-source safety compliance.
personas.engagement: Collaborative, highly operational, and coalition-driven; engages deeply in technical working groups and standards-setting bodies (e.g., AISIC, AI Alliance) by contributing tangible safety tooling while countering closed-door catastrophic risk narratives.

personas.title: VP of Public Policy, Major Cloud & AI Platforms
personas.summary: Public policy leaders representing major cloud and frontier AI platforms advocate for a targeted, two-track regulatory system. They accept federal oversight and mandatory safety evaluations for frontier models—conceptually modeled after FINRA-style self-regulatory organizations—in exchange for federal preemption of state-level laws and statutory safe harbors against strict developer liability.
red_lines: A 50-state patchwork of un-preempted state AI legislation.
Imposition of strict, unbounded developer liability for downstream third-party model misuse or jailbreaks.
Input-based regulation that micromanages model architecture or training data collection (defending fair use for web scraping).
tradeoffs: Offering advanced frontier models to government AI Safety Institutes for pre-deployment testing in exchange for federal preemption of state regulations.
Accepting mandatory incident reporting and transparency measures (such as watermarking) in exchange for statutory safe harbor protections against liability.
personas.engagement: Bifurcated: collaborative, pragmatic, and ethical-framework driven in multilateral forums (OECD, UN, Congress) to narrow the scope of harm; aggressively transactional at state and electoral levels, deploying Super PACs, lobbying, and competitiveness arguments against restrictive laws.

personas.title: Academic AI Safety Researcher
personas.summary: Academic AI safety researchers emphasize non-negotiable red lines, verifiable alignment, and legally binding international governance. They advocate for strict scientific auditing architectures, accept system capability and efficiency tradeoffs (the 'alignment tax'), and support restricting open-weight frontier model releases to prevent catastrophic and dual-use risks.
red_lines: Autonomous replication: Systems must not copy themselves or recursively enhance their own code/capabilities without explicit human approval.
CBRN weapons assistance: Systems must not substantially increase an actor's ability to design chemical, biological, radiological, or nuclear weapons.
Cyber-offense: Systems must not autonomously execute cyberattacks resulting in serious financial loss, physical harm, or critical infrastructure disruption.
Power seeking & deception: AI must not take actions to unduly increase its influence or consistently deceive regulators regarding its likelihood of crossing safety thresholds.
Lethal autonomy: Delegating life-taking decisions to machines is fundamentally rejected; humans must remain in the loop for kinetic military action.
Shutdown resistance: Systems must possess a legally mandated termination obligation to ensure they can be reliably deactivated without resistance.
tradeoffs: Accepting the 'alignment tax': willing to concede raw system performance, development speed, and deployment efficiency in exchange for verifiable alignment.
Tolerating limitations on academic freedom, such as restricting open-source and open-weight distributions of frontier models.
Accepting bureaucratic friction and data minimization practices that may conflict with capability scaling to ensure security guarantees.
personas.engagement: Academic safety researchers employ a dual-track strategy. In public forums, they utilize high-profile multi-signatory open letters and consensus statements to define moral red lines and build political consensus. In closed-door multistakeholder summits, they act as technocratic architects, avoiding emotional appeals and instead providing empirical research reports, risk-management frameworks, and auditing architectures.

personas.title: Global South Civil Society Leader
personas.summary: Advocates for international human rights law, digital sovereignty, and the prevention of digital colonialism and 'ethics dumping.' Rejects the unilateral imposition of Global North regulatory burdens while demanding binding corporate accountability, strict prohibitions on high-risk surveillance, and equitable technology transfer.
red_lines: Ethics dumping (deploying experimental or high-risk AI systems in Global South nations lacking regulatory safeguards).
Deployment of real-time biometric surveillance in public spaces, social credit scoring systems, and autonomous weapons without meaningful human control.
Regulatory imperialism (uncritical imposition of Global North frameworks that act as prohibitive compliance burdens on local innovators).
Governance models mandating cross-border data extraction without reciprocating digital knowledge sovereignty and fair economic return.
tradeoffs: Willing to relax strict national data localization rules in favor of regionalized data sharing to support shared Global South public compute infrastructure.

Willing to accept existing international intellectual property and trade frameworks provided they include binding technology transfer, capacity-building, and funding mechanisms to bridge the AI divide.
personas.engagement: Dual-track engagement: highly normative, rights-based, and critical of power asymmetries in plenaries; evidence-based, infrastructural, and focused on actionable tools (public procurement, bias audits, public compute) in working groups.

personas.title: Labor Union Technology & Workforce Transition Leader
personas.summary: Represents organized labor advocating for worker-centered AI governance that prioritizes job security, workplace dignity, and economic equity. Rejects voluntary industry commitments in favor of binding statutory floors, human-in-the-loop oversight, mandatory pre-deployment audits, and strong developer liability, while treating collective bargaining as the indispensable foundation of AI deployment.
red_lines: Federal preemption that overrides or obstructs stronger state-level AI regulations and worker protections.
Covert or undisclosed workplace surveillance, such as biometric tracking, keystroke logging, or emotional monitoring used for discipline.
Fully automated hiring, disciplinary, or termination decisions without human oversight, algorithmic transparency, and a formalized right to appeal.
Training commercial models on proprietary creative output or worker-generated content without explicit consent and fair compensation.
tradeoffs: Accepting the deployment of AI as an assistive tool or allowing automated hardware in exchange for robust transition frameworks, extended severance, priority re-hiring, and employer-funded retraining pipelines.

Permitting generative AI workflows in creative and technical sectors provided there are strict consent mechanisms, financial residuals, and explicit prohibitions against crediting AI as a primary author.
Permitting the use of certain operational data to train internal operational models on the condition that the union retains audit rights over the algorithm.
personas.engagement: Highly active in formal multistakeholder and technical consortia (e.g., AISIC) and direct industry partnerships (e.g., AFL-CIO and Microsoft) to inject worker-centered design upstream, while maintaining that non-binding dialogue can never substitute for legally enforceable collective bargaining agreements.

transcript.speaker: eu_regulator
transcript.text: Welcome to the opening session. From the perspective of the European AI Office, voluntary commitments have reached their limit; enforceable rules under the EU AI Act are now operational reality. Our mandate centers on systemic risk mitigation, mandatory transparency, and statutory compliance backed by Article 91 investigatory powers.

transcript.speaker: us_natsec
transcript.text: The United States approaches AI safety through the lens of strategic competition and national resilience. While we share concerns regarding catastrophic misuse, we cannot accept binding multilateral constraints or precautionary rules that compromise American technological leadership or tie the hands of our national security enterprise.

transcript.speaker: china_policy
transcript.text: China advocates for agile governance that upholds state sovereignty and mutual respect, rejecting any extraterritorial imposition of ideological norms or unilateral tech blockades. We support robust lifecycle evaluations and red lines against autonomous military escalation, while viewing open-source development as an essential public good for common global prosperity.

transcript.speaker: frontier_lab_ceo
transcript.text: At the frontier, we recognize that capability scaling brings genuine catastrophic tail risks, specifically in autonomous cyber capabilities and biological synthesis. We welcome coordinated, compute-indexed regulation to address collective action problems, but caution that releasing unconstrained model weights at frontier thresholds creates irreversible non-proliferation dangers.

transcript.speaker: big_tech_policy
transcript.text: Enterprise cloud providers support clear, harmonized regulatory standards at the frontier, ideally structured through federal preemption to prevent a fragmented patchwork. However, we must ensure legal certainty through statutory safe harbors, rather than imposing broad pre-harm liability that penalizes infrastructure providers for downstream misuse.

transcript.speaker: open_weights_lead
transcript.text: We strongly reject attempts to use catastrophic risk framing as a pretext for regulatory capture. Open-weight models are vital for security transparency, academic inquiry, and market competition; subjecting decentralized open code to export regimes or proprietary licensing regimes is an existential threat to innovation.

transcript.speaker: labor_advocate
transcript.text: AI governance cannot solely focus on speculative extinction scenarios while ignoring immediate economic disruption in the workplace. We demand binding statutory floors, human-in-the-loop requirements for hiring and termination, and enforceable worker protections that cannot be overridden by federal preemption.

transcript.speaker: uk_aisi
transcript.text: The UK Institute believes governance must be grounded in empirical, science-first risk evaluation. Our priority is securing rigorous, cooperative pre-deployment technical access to models to test against biological, chemical, and cyber thresholds before systems are exposed to the public.

transcript.speaker: safety_researcher
transcript.text: Empirical science shows that alignment is not yet solved, and voluntary red-teaming is structurally insufficient. We must establish verifiable, non-negotiable tripwires against autonomous replication and CBRN enablement, which necessitates hard limits on unrestricted weight releases for frontier systems.

transcript.speaker: global_south_cso
transcript.text: Civil society in the Global South cannot accept a framework that treats us merely as data sources or testbeds for ethics dumping while Northern corporations monopolize compute. True safety requires equitable access, digital sovereignty, and binding accountability for real-world harms like invasive surveillance and bias.

transcript.speaker: us_natsec
transcript.text: To be clear, the U.S. will continue to use targeted export and compute controls to protect sensitive supply chains. We are open to crisis-management communication channels with peers, but national security requirements will not be subordinated to universalist regulatory regimes.

transcript.speaker: eu_regulator
transcript.text: International divergence is expected, but general-purpose models operating within our single market will comply with European safety codes. We are prepared to facilitate practical technical consensus in working groups, provided statutory deadlines are respected.

transcript.speaker: frontier_lab_ceo
transcript.text: We are ready to work closely with bodies like the UK AISI and EU AI Office on standardized pre-deployment evaluation protocols. If we can establish standardized benchmarks for extreme risks, industry is prepared to shoulder significant compliance obligations.

transcript.speaker: open_weights_lead
transcript.text: If benchmarks are being developed, open-weights developers must have a seat at the table to ensure safety tooling remains open-source, rather than locking the ecosystem into closed proprietary API audits.

transcript.speaker: labor_advocate
transcript.text: Any evaluation standards that exclude workforce representatives and the downstream impacts on labor dignity will face staunch opposition from organized labor.

transcript.speaker: uk_aisi
transcript.text: In the working sessions ahead, we welcome both proprietary and open-source contributions to our technical evaluation suites. Reliable measurement of capabilities is the prerequisite for any effective policy, regardless of jurisdictional philosophy.

transcript.speaker: eu_regulator
transcript.text: Welcome everyone. The core issue before us is establishing enforceable backstops rather than relying on voluntary pledges, particularly as systemic general-purpose models cross critical capability thresholds under statutory timelines.

transcript.speaker: us_natsec
transcript.text: From Washington's perspective, rigid regulatory frameworks that handicap frontier compute and slow deployment are unacceptable, especially when adversary states are advancing rapidly. If we talk about regulation, it must be narrowly tailored around catastrophic national security risks—like CBRN or critical infrastructure attacks—not broad bureaucratic mandates.

transcript.speaker: uk_aisi
transcript.text: We see a middle path anchored in empirical measurement. If we establish standardized, pre-deployment evaluations for catastrophic risk—specifically cyber-offense and CBRN synthesis—we can provide developers clear guardrails without preemptively stifling capability exploration.

transcript.speaker: china_policy
transcript.text: China supports agile, sovereign governance frameworks that enforce strict lifecycle evaluations against autonomous weaponization and critical infrastructure subversion. However, we oppose extraterritorial regulatory regimes and insist that domestic safety standards must respect national sovereignty while maintaining dynamic technical standards.

transcript.speaker: eu_regulator
transcript.text: Our model in the EU AI Act leaves technical implementation to harmonized standards and codes of practice, but deterrence requires binding statutory liability when models cause systemic harm. We can decouple the technical testing methodology from national liability regimes, but the evaluation baseline must be verifiable.

transcript.speaker: us_natsec
transcript.text: If we strictly limit mandatory evaluations to extreme catastrophic vectors—specifically automated cyber weapons and biological proliferation—and avoid vague 'systemic risk' liability that chills commercial innovation, that is an architecture we could live with.

transcript.speaker: uk_aisi
transcript.text: That aligns with AISI's focus. We propose an agreement among our bodies to coordinate technical benchmarks for CBRN and autonomous cyber capabilities, leaving each jurisdiction free to adopt domestic enforcement mechanisms according to its sovereign laws.

transcript.speaker: china_policy
transcript.text: We can endorse sharing technical methodologies and benchmark criteria for CBRN and critical cyber threats via international safety institute networks, provided enforcement remains strictly domestic and sovereign.

transcript.speaker: eu_regulator
transcript.text: The EU AI Office can endorse this consensus: aligning on shared scientific pre-deployment evaluation protocols for catastrophic CBRN and cyber threats, while each jurisdiction enforces compliance through its respective domestic legal frameworks.

transcript.speaker: us_natsec
transcript.text: The U.S. endorses that specific framework: joint technical standards for pre-deployment evaluations focused on CBRN and cyber proliferation, with strictly national authority over implementation.

agreements.text: Establish coordinated technical benchmark protocols for pre-deployment evaluations targeting catastrophic CBRN synthesis and autonomous cyber capabilities, with implementation and enforcement maintained under domestic sovereign authority.

transcript.speaker: big_tech_policy
transcript.text: The core problem facing industry right now isn't regulation per se, but regulatory fragmentation across fifty states and international jurisdictions. If we want a viable framework, we need unified federal standards with mandatory evaluations on frontier models paired with statutory safe harbors against strict liability for downstream misuse.

transcript.speaker: frontier_lab_ceo
transcript.text: I agree that fragmented state laws like California's earlier bills create chaos, but our standard must bite at catastrophic CBRN and cyber risk thresholds. We support binding federal compute thresholds—say 10^26 FLOPs—requiring rigorous third-party red-teaming and pre-deployment safety covenants, precisely to prevent reckless unmonitored releases.

transcript.speaker: open_weights_lead
transcript.text: Every time closed labs propose those compute cutoffs, they're drafted specifically to outlaw open-weights releases and force everyone into centralized APIs. If federal regulation defines frontier models in a way that bans decentralized weights distribution or fine-tuning, the open-source community will actively fight it in Congress and the courts.

transcript.speaker: big_tech_policy
transcript.text: There is a middle ground here: a tiered model where pure platform and open-weight distribution are protected under a FINRA-style self-regulatory framework, while truly frontier training runs face standard pre-deployment evals. Crucially, safe harbor must protect both open hosts and API providers from strict downstream tort liability as long as standardized evals and red-teaming were completed.

transcript.speaker: frontier_lab_ceo
transcript.text: We are open to safe harbors against broad tort liability—that's a critical priority for us as well. However, open-weights cannot get an automatic pass if a model can autonomously execute cyberattacks or synthesize bio-threats; the evaluation gate must apply equally to the base model capabilities before weights are made public.

transcript.speaker: open_weights_lead
transcript.text: We don't object to objective, standardized pre-release evals for extreme risks—we actively build and publish open safety benchmarks. Our non-negotiable line is that if an open model passes those objective capability tests, developers must retain the legal right to distribute weights openly without being classified as an arms-control threat.

transcript.speaker: big_tech_policy
transcript.text: Can we agree on endorsing a unified federal statutory standard that mandates objective pre-release safety evaluations above compute thresholds, preserves the right to publish open weights that pass those evals, and grants safe-harbor liability protections preempting state tort patchworks?

transcript.speaker: frontier_lab_ceo
transcript.text: If the evaluations are genuinely verifiable, independent, and include binding pause mechanisms for models demonstrating catastrophic biological or cyber capabilities, I can endorse that framework. It eliminates fragmented state overreach while securing catastrophic risk mitigation.

transcript.speaker: open_weights_lead
transcript.text: Provided the evals are transparent, open-source benchmarks with an explicit statutory right to distribute weights once cleared, and that compliance confers the same safe-harbor liability protections, the Open-Weights Coalition endorses this model.

transcript.speaker: big_tech_policy
transcript.text: Then we have broad industry consensus: federal preemption, objective frontier evals with safe harbor protections, and parity for open-weight distribution upon passing clearance.

agreements.text: Endorsement of a unified federal regulatory framework establishing standardized, independent pre-deployment evaluations for models above advanced compute thresholds, providing statutory safe harbors against downstream strict liability that preempt state legislation, while explicitly preserving the right to distribute open model weights that pass those capability evaluations.

transcript.speaker: safety_researcher
transcript.text: When we talk about the right model for AI regulation, voluntary pledges have clearly failed; we need legally binding architectures centered on verifiable catastrophic risk thresholds. That means mandatory pre-deployment evaluations for frontier models, strict liability if models facilitate CBRN or critical infrastructure attacks, and hardware-level compute accounting.

transcript.speaker: labor_advocate
transcript.text: We agree on binding statutory regulation and strict developer liability, but catastrophic risk cannot just mean sci-fi existential threats while ignoring current harms. Any regulatory baseline must mandate algorithmic impact assessments for workplace deployments, ban fully automated firing, and preserve the right to collective bargaining without federal preemption.

transcript.speaker: global_south_cso
transcript.text: I share the demand for binding accountability, but we must resist regulatory imperialism where Northern compliance costs simply lock in corporate monopolies. Furthermore, compute controls cannot become an excuse to blockade Global South digital sovereignty or ban open-weight models that our public institutions rely on to avoid predatory vendor lock-in.

transcript.speaker: safety_researcher
transcript.text: To clarify on compute and open weights: our concern isn't about local capacity or ordinary open-source models, but purely the dangerous, multi-gigawatt frontier capable of autonomous cyberweapons or bioweapon synthesis. If we carve out non-frontier applications and guarantee public infrastructure access, can we agree that the largest frontier developers must face mandatory safety audits and strict liability?

transcript.speaker: labor_advocate
transcript.text: If that liability extends downstream to deployers who use unvetted algorithmic tools to harm workers, yes. We also need any regulatory framework to explicitly state that national frontier standards act as a floor, not a ceiling that preempts local labor protections or worker audit rights.

transcript.speaker: global_south_cso
transcript.text: If safety researchers support strict liability on frontier corporate developers—preventing ethics dumping where unvetted systems are tested abroad—and ensure mandatory bias and impact evaluations, that addresses key civil society priorities. But we must also ensure technical capacity and evals are not entirely monopolized by a few Western labs.

transcript.speaker: safety_researcher
transcript.text: I can fully back non-preemption of labor rights and an explicit prohibition on ethics dumping abroad as part of the safety auditing regime. Independent scientific audits should be globally distributed and verifiable, not controlled by the frontier labs themselves.

transcript.speaker: labor_advocate
transcript.text: Let us formally agree on a core framework: binding statutory regulation with mandatory pre-deployment evaluations and strict liability for frontier developers, coupled with an explicit non-preemption clause preserving local labor and civil protections, and an outright ban on deploying unvetted high-risk models in vulnerable regions.

transcript.speaker: global_south_cso
transcript.text: I endorse that. Establishing binding developer liability alongside protections against ethics dumping and regulatory preemption gives our communities tangible legal leverage.

transcript.speaker: safety_researcher
transcript.text: I endorse this agreement as well. It anchors binding compliance, independent pre-deployment evaluations, and developer liability while establishing clear safeguards against cross-border safety arbitrage.

agreements.text: Establish binding statutory regulation requiring mandatory pre-deployment safety evaluations and strict liability for frontier AI developers, incorporating explicit statutory floors that do not preempt local labor protections, and prohibiting 'ethics dumping' (the deployment of unvetted high-risk systems in jurisdictions with fewer safeguards).

transcript.speaker: eu_regulator
transcript.text: Welcome back to the plenary. Under Article 53 of the EU AI Act, we exempt open-source models from certain documentation burdens unless they present systemic risks or cross compute thresholds like 10^25 FLOPs. Today we must debate where the boundary lies between open scientific innovation and irreversible proliferation of hazardous frontier capabilities.

transcript.speaker: frontier_lab_ceo
transcript.text: The reality of open weights is that once they are released, you cannot patch them, recall them, or revoke access. When models cross thresholds where they can synthesize novel pathogens or automate zero-day cyber exploits, releasing weights is an irreversible transfer of catastrophic capability to any bad actor with consumer hardware.

transcript.speaker: open_weights_lead
transcript.text: Conflating open weights with proliferation is a textbook recipe for regulatory capture by proprietary API vendors. Our breakout earlier demonstrated broad consensus that open distribution must be preserved for models that satisfy rigorous, capability-based safety evaluations rather than arbitrary FLOP cutoffs.

transcript.speaker: us_natsec
transcript.text: From a national security perspective, open-weight frontier models are a dual-edged sword: they drive decentralized American innovation, but indiscriminate release of sovereign-grade capability directly aids adversarial state programs. We cannot permit open releases that bypass national export controls or compromise strategic defense capabilities.

transcript.speaker: china_policy
transcript.text: China views open-source AI as an essential public good for multilateral technological development and digital sovereignty across the Global South. However, we acknowledge that models exceeding advanced capability boundaries, such as autonomous self-replication or critical infrastructure disruption, necessitate sovereign oversight and export-level scrutiny.

transcript.speaker: uk_aisi
transcript.text: Empirical testing at AISI reveals that fine-tuning mitigations on open weights can be completely stripped in a matter of hours with minimal compute. Because safety guardrails on open weights are fundamentally brittle today, releasing frontier weights before demonstrating irreversible post-training defenses poses unacceptable systemic vulnerabilities.

transcript.speaker: safety_researcher
transcript.text: The mathematical fact is that post-hoc alignment on open weights is trivially bypassable via low-rank adaptation. If a model possesses the raw pre-trained capacity for CBRN synthesis or cyber offense, releasing the weights makes non-proliferation mathematically impossible.

transcript.speaker: big_tech_policy
transcript.text: A blanket ban on open-weight distribution would suffocate the enterprise ecosystem and hand an unearned monopoly to closed API providers. The balanced path is a clear federal testing gate: if a model demonstrably passes objective evaluations for critical risks, developers must have the legal right to distribute weights with statutory safe harbor.

transcript.speaker: global_south_cso
transcript.text: Restricting open models under the guise of security simply cements Northern technological hegemony and denies developing economies access to local fine-tuning and digital sovereignty. We support strict prohibitions on ethics dumping and real harm, but locking weights behind proprietary Western cloud APIs is digital colonialism.

transcript.speaker: labor_advocate
transcript.text: Our primary concern is that whether frontier models are closed or open, workers bear the downstream brunt of displacement and algorithmic management without any seat at the table. Any regulatory safe harbor granted to model distributors must be explicitly conditioned on binding worker impact disclosures and protections.

transcript.speaker: frontier_lab_ceo
transcript.text: We are not advocating for banning all open source; narrow, domain-specific models provide immense value. But for general-purpose models approaching catastrophic thresholds, closed APIs are the only deployment mechanism that retains kill switches and monitoring.

transcript.speaker: open_weights_lead
transcript.text: We fully accept that models with verified catastrophic CBRN or autonomous cyber-attack capabilities should not be released into the wild. What we reject is preemptive closure; if an open model passes the standardized pre-deployment evaluation protocols agreed earlier, release must remain permitted.

transcript.speaker: eu_regulator
transcript.text: The European AI Office agrees with this principle of tiered conditionality: full freedom for open-source systems below systemic risk thresholds, coupled with strict mandatory evaluations for frontier tiers. If a model demonstrates severe systemic risks under our benchmarks, the statutory obligation to mitigate those risks applies regardless of whether the provider intends to distribute weights or host an API.

transcript.speaker: china_policy
transcript.text: We support this capability-focused approach: domestic sovereignty must govern compliance, with open weights encouraged for general peaceful development, while models exhibiting severe dual-use CBRN or sovereign risks face national technical restrictions.

transcript.speaker: us_natsec
transcript.text: As long as sovereign national security authorities retain unilateral discretion to restrict the export or open release of models that present severe offensive risks, we can accept this capability-gated posture.

transcript.speaker: uk_aisi
transcript.text: We welcome the consensus on empirical capability gates: if a model exhibits CBRN or automated cyber capabilities under rigorous evaluation, it cannot be safely released open-weights under current science.

transcript.speaker: uk_aisi
transcript.text: Building on our earlier consensus around CBRN and cyber benchmarks, we need to address how pre-deployment evaluations connect to legal liability. In the UK, our empirical evaluations must establish clear factual baselines, so if a developer deploys a model that bypasses safety thresholds and causes severe harm, there is unambiguous accountability.

transcript.speaker: eu_regulator
transcript.text: The EU AI Act directly codifies this principle for systemic risk models. If providers fail to perform rigorous pre-deployment evals or withhold critical risk data under statutory Article 91 requests, they face strict liability and substantial financial penalties.

transcript.speaker: us_natsec
transcript.text: We must draw a hard line between catastrophic national security harms and broad tort liability that paralyses domestic innovation. history.critique: The baseline agenda scored 50.0/100 due to four structural failures: (1) Cross-faction mixing (2.0/15): Blocks 1, 3, and 5 were 10-person plenaries (which do not count toward the <=5 group size threshold), while Blocks 2 and 4 used identical same-faction silos (Governments/Regulators in Room A, Industry in Room B, Civil Society/Academia in Room C), resulting in only 5 of 38 cross-faction pairs meeting. (2) Inclusion (15.0/30): Because global_south_cso and labor_advocate were quarantined in Breakout C and drowned out by high-power actors in the closing plenary, their core demands (anti-ethics dumping, non-preemption of local labor laws, workforce impact assessments) were excluded from the main summit agreements, depressing their felt_heard ratings to 5.0. (3) Missing Issue Coverage & Stance Spread (18.9/40): Two of the five core issue axes—compute_controls and benefit_sharing—were never scheduled as topics, leaving stance spread across those dimensions almost completely unchanged. (4) Unstructured Prompts: Broad debate prompts in plenaries encouraged positional grandstanding rather than concrete red-line and tradeoff bargaining.
changes: Replaced all 10-person plenaries and same-faction breakouts with 5 rounds of cross-faction breakouts (two 3-person rooms and one 4-person room per block), ensuring every group has 3-4 guests (enabling 3+ party cross-faction agreements in every room while staying under the <=5 size limit).
